title: Orcas Are Smashing Sunfish Like Piñatas — and Scientists Filmed It
summary: Have you ever whacked a piñata at a birthday party? Now imagine a killer whale doing that — to a fish. Scientists filmed something wild in the Gulf of California in 2024 and 2025. One adult orca held a dead sharp-tail sunfish steady. A second orca slammed into it so hard the sunfish exploded into pieces. Sunfish are huge — they can grow up to about 10 feet long. That's longer than a school bus is wide. Orcas, also called killer whales, are famous for clever hunting tricks. They slap stingrays, punt seals into the air, and even work as a team to knock penguins off ice. But this? This was new. "I was absolutely gobsmacked," says Marianne Nyegaard, a marine biologist at Auckland Museum in New Zealand who didn't work on the study. "I thought it was the coolest thing I had ever seen." So why do orcas do it? One idea: they're breaking the big fish into smaller bites so young orcas can eat. After one explosion, a young orca fed on the pieces. Another idea: it's just fun. Orcas are super social animals. A single activity can feed them, help them bond, and teach young whales how to hunt. Scientists published the findings in July. Next up: watching for more piñata moments.
why_it_matters: This shows that teamwork and play matter for many animals, not just people — and that even scientists can still be surprised by nature.

background_read: Orcas — also called killer whales — live in every ocean and usually swim in family groups led by older females.
They are famous for clever hunting tricks, such as slapping stingrays or knocking penguins off ice.
Auckland Museum, in New Zealand, is a large museum with natural-history collections, and it is where Marianne Nyegaard works.
Article_Structure: WHO: Scientists filming orcas, plus marine biologist Marianne Nyegaard, who watched the videos and commented
WHAT: One adult orca held a dead sharp-tail sunfish steady while a second orca slammed into it so hard the fish exploded into pieces
WHERE: The Gulf of California, in 2024 and 2025
WHY: It might be a way to break food into bites for young orcas, or simply a fun, social activity for the group

perspectives.description: This is a brand-new hunting trick we have never seen before, and it is exciting to finally have it on film.
The orcas might just be having fun, since they are very social animals that often do things together as a group.
We only have a few videos so far, so we can't yet say for sure why orcas do this or how often it happens.
